title: American English vs. British English (part 2)
main_content:
[This article is divided into 2 parts! In part 1 we discussed some differences between British English and American English.]

But the real fun begins when we start exploring idioms and expressions that are unique to each country.

Let’s start with “Bob’s your uncle.” To an American ear, that is a weird expression. And it has nothing to do with any relative you may or may not have named Bob. It is just a way to finish a set of simple instructions.

What is the different but equal saying in the U.S.? Americans might say, “and there you have it!” Or sometimes, more dramatic people will say, “Ta-da!”

If a British person says, “I’ve got the hump,” it means they are annoyed or upset. In the U.S., some informal ways to say we are upset are “I’m ticked off” or “I’m miffed.”

Now, when Americans are really surprised by something, we can say we “are at a loss for words.”  Or more informally, we simply say we are “shocked” or “blown away.”

Across the Atlantic in the U.K., they are “gobsmacked.”

Finally, a familiar word used by both countries but in different ways is “cheers.”  We use the word over drinks when we are wishing someone good health or congratulating. The British use “cheers” to mean “thank you.”  For that, we Americans say, “Thank you!”

questions.question: What can an American person say when he or she finishes giving instructions?
options: We’re at a loss for words.

questions.question: If someone says he or she is gobsmacked how does this person feel?
If someone says “cheers” instead of “thank you,” is this person American or British?
